chunks: "Take an NPN. It's an N-type emitter, a very thin P-type base, and an N-type collector. In normal operation I forward-bias the base-emitter junction, about 0.
7 volts, and reverse-bias the base-collector junction. The forward bias lowers the barrier at the emitter junction, so electrons from the heavily doped emitter flow into the base.
In the base they're minority carriers. Because the base is so thin, around a tenth to a micron, most of them diffuse across it before they recombine with holes.
When they reach the edge of the base-collector depletion region, the strong field there, which comes from the reverse bias, sweeps them into the collector.
That electron flow from emitter to collector is the collector current, and it depends on how many electrons the emitter injects, which is set by V BE , not on V CE .
That's why I C equals I Se to the V BE over V T and why the output curves are flat. A small fraction of the carriers don't make it.
A few electrons recombine with holes in the base, and some holes from the base are injected back into the emitter. The base current is what resupplies those holes.
Since the base is thin and the emitter heavily doped, both losses are small, around one percent, so I B is about I C over 100 . That's the current gain.
So the transistor is basically a controlled flow of carriers from emitter to collector, with the base as a thin valve whose control signal is the forward bias on the junction."
